Lesson 5 · Anticipate next week

Multiple regression, interactions, and inference

The simple line connects longer delivery times with greater stockout pressure. The director now asks for comparisons that reflect the different environments in which stores operate.

Business question → General theory → Worked application → Synthesis

First learn the definitions, notation, and logic of the method. Then use the shared case to work through the calculation and its interpretation.

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

The motivating question

An urban store running frequent promotions may face a different workload from another store with the same delivery cycle. We will extend the existing regression to include location, demand, and promotion exposure, then allow the delivery-time slope to differ by location. The output is a set of specified store profiles that operations can use for planning. We keep the same rows and outcome as Lesson 4.

Define adjusted comparisons and joint questions

General theory

Multiple regression holds the other included predictors fixed

Y = β₀ + β₁X₁ + … + βₖXₖ + u

Ordinary least squares chooses coefficients to minimize the sum of squared residuals. A coefficient describes changing its predictor while holding the other specified predictors fixed. With interactions or powers, read the associated terms together. The design row records every input used in a prediction; the appendix shows its matrix representation.

Overlapping predictors make separate coefficient estimates less precise

Classical relationship: VIF=1/(1−R²); SE multiplier=√VIF
R² from predicting one input with the othersVariance inflationSE multiplier
0.0011
0.7542
0.96255

Multicollinearity means inputs carry overlapping information. Holding residual variance and that input’s total variation fixed, VIF describes how much coefficient variance increases compared with orthogonal predictors. Exact redundancy prevents unique coefficients; near redundancy inflates uncertainty. It does not by itself bias OLS or prove poor prediction. Inspect whether the intended separate comparisons are supported by the observed combinations.

A joint test asks whether several restrictions hold together

  • One test: are the two delivery slopes equal?
  • Joint test: are both group intercept and slope differences zero?
  • Coincident lines require both restrictions
  • Evaluate the coefficient vector with its covariance

In a model a+bX+cD+dXD, equal slopes means d=0. Coincident group lines means c=d=0. Two separate non-rejections are not a substitute for a joint test. A classical F test compares nested residual sums of squares under constant variance; a robust Wald test uses the HC1 covariance. The application reports the robust joint result and the appendix shows both calculations.

Omitted-variable changes combine an outcome association with sorting

b short = b long + γ × δ

Fit Y on X, then Y on X and Z on the same observations. γ is Z’s coefficient in the longer regression; δ comes from regressing Z on X. Their product exactly explains the sample slope change. This is an algebraic comparison of regressions. Interpreting a coefficient as the effect of an intervention requires the design developed later in the course.

Connect the foundations before calculating

General theory

Holding controls fixed means comparing their remaining variation

  • Regress delivery X on all the other columns Z
  • Regress outcome Y on the same columns Z
  • Regress the remaining Y on the remaining X
  • The residual slope equals the full-model X coefficient

This is the partial-regression construction. Include an intercept in Z. Removing Z from both variables isolates the variation available for the X coefficient. Residualizing only the outcome is insufficient. In the six-column model Z includes urban, demand, promotions and delivery×urban, so the construction targets the delivery main coefficient, interpreted at urban=0. It is a projection identity, not proof that these controls identify a causal effect.

Dependence determines which uncertainty calculation is defensible

Changing the covariance calculation does not change the OLS coefficients
Observed structureUncertainty methodRequirement
Independent, equal-variance errorsClassical covarianceCorrect mean and sampling conditions
Independent, unequal-variance errorsRobust covarianceEnough independent observations
Repeated outcomes within storesCluster by storeEnough independent store clusters

A robust covariance accounts for varying spread; clustering additionally permits dependence within the named group. If delivery teams link stores, clustering only by store may miss shared shocks. Few clusters require special care. These choices support uncertainty about an estimable comparison and do not establish its causal identification.

Encode the comparisons the model should allow

General theory

K categories use K−1 indicators when an intercept is present

Alternative categorical coding of the same delivery variable
Delivery categoryD3D4D5
2 days: reference000
3 days100
4 days010
5 days001

Each indicator coefficient compares its category with the two-day reference, holding other terms fixed. The reference observations remain in the fit. Including all four indicators plus an intercept duplicates one column. This is an alternative to a single numeric delivery slope; do not add redundant columns merely to enlarge a model.

Interactions let a group difference change with the predictor

For Y=a+bX+cD+dXD, group D=0 has line a+bX and group D=1 has line (a+c)+(b+d)X. The difference at X is c+dX. Dropping c forces the lines to share an intercept at X=0, which is a substantive restriction. For two continuous inputs, Y=a+bX+cZ+dXZ gives an X slope of b+dZ. Centering X at a meaningful value moves the reference comparison without changing fitted values.

Curvature and interactions answer different questions about changing slopes

Interpret the complete expression at specified values
Term addedSlope in XQuestion
qX²b+2qXDoes the slope change with X?
dXZb+dZDoes the slope change with Z?

Lesson 4 introduced curved relationships. Multiple regression combines them with measured controls. With centered demand d=D−100 and term q(d/10)², the demand slope is b_d+2qd/100 in rate points per demand-index unit. For a continuous interaction with coefficients b=.5 and d=.2, the X slope is .5 at Z=0 and .9 at Z=2; these are illustrative coefficients, not retail estimates.

Quantify uncertainty in a regression relationship

General theory

A coefficient and its standard error answer different questions

  • Coefficient: size and direction of the fitted comparison
  • Standard error: sampling variation of that estimate
  • Interval: a range of values compatible with the procedure
  • Test: compare the estimate with a stated benchmark

The coefficient estimates a population regression relationship. Its standard error describes how the estimator varies across samples under the analysis model. A precise estimate need not be large enough to matter operationally. Begin by naming the coefficient, its units, and the comparison being estimated.

A test measures the distance from a benchmark in standard-error units

Statistic = (b − β₀) / SE(b); interval = b ± critical value × SE(b)

For a two-sided test, the null specifies β=β₀ and the alternative allows values on either side. Under the null, compare the statistic with its reference distribution; the p-value is its two-tail probability at least this far from zero. It is not the probability that the null is true. A matching two-sided 5% test rejects exactly when the corresponding 95% interval excludes β₀. A 99% interval is wider and corresponds to a 1% test. Classical normal-error OLS uses Student t with n−p degrees of freedom; the robust examples here use a large-sample normal reference.

More information narrows uncertainty when the model is held fixed

  • More independent observations improve precision
  • More predictor spread helps distinguish a slope
  • Less unexplained outcome spread reduces standard errors
  • Overlapping predictors make separate slopes harder to distinguish

In simple classical OLS, SE(b)=s/√Σ(X−X̄)². Here s²=SSE/(n−2), so residual variation raises uncertainty and predictor variation lowers it. The formula does not promise that collecting arbitrary extra rows or changing the population improves the same estimand. The appendix derives the slope and intercept calculations.

Robust standard errors change uncertainty without changing the fitted line

Choose the covariance estimate, then use it consistently
ChoiceVariance modelSame OLS coefficients?
ClassicalConstant residual varianceYes
HC1 robustVariance may differ across independent storesYes

Heteroskedasticity means unequal error variance across input profiles. HC1 estimates coefficient covariance using squared residuals with a degrees-of-freedom correction. HC3 uses a different leverage correction; the original deck used HC3. This course retains HC1 to keep all displayed coefficients, intervals, and contrasts on one convention. Robust covariance does not repair a misspecified mean equation or define the variance of a future individual outcome.

Distinguish a mean response from one new outcome

General theory

A mean interval and an individual interval target different quantities

Use the same profile and outcome period for both
TargetUncertainty included
E[Y | X=x]Estimation of the mean relationship
A new Y at X=xMean estimation plus individual variation

An individual prediction interval adds the new observation’s variation around its conditional mean. In this lesson one outcome is a store’s eight-week baseline-average rate, not one product-day or next week’s rate. With the same variance model and confidence level, an individual interval is wider than a mean interval.

Classical mean uncertainty widens away from the predictor mean

SE(mean at x) = s √[1/n + (x−X̄)²/Sxx]

Sxx=Σ(X−X̄)². Under constant residual variance, the mean standard error is smallest at X̄, where the second term vanishes. For a new individual, add 1 inside the square root. More data can make mean uncertainty small, while individual variation remains. These are pointwise intervals at each x, not a simultaneous confidence statement about the entire curve.

A model’s scope follows the stores, period, and measurement it represents

  • Name the population and outcome period
  • Check that new profiles have comparable inputs
  • Look for changes in operating conditions
  • Evaluate later outcomes before expanding use

External validity concerns transferring a result to another setting. A baseline relationship for these stores does not automatically describe a new store format or a different supply network. Ask what similarities and new evidence support the transfer. This is an operating choice about where the model can help, rather than another coefficient test.

Keep the same outcome and analysis rows

Worked application

The comparison uses the same 150 baseline store profiles

All models below use the same store-level rows
InputMeaning
OutcomeStockout rate over weeks 1–8 (%)
Lead / urbanUsual delivery days / 0–1 location
Demand−100Observed baseline demand above reference
Promotion shareFraction of baseline weeks promoted
Lead×urbanAllows the delivery slope to differ

We retain the Lesson 4 outcome and sample. A promotion share of .25 means promotions in a quarter of baseline weeks. These are explanatory baseline inputs; Lesson 6 will specify what is available before a forecast is issued. Keeping the sample fixed makes changes between nested models interpretable.

Construct complete adjusted profiles

Worked application

The richer equation includes every input used by the profile

Rate = b₀ + b₁lead + b₂urban + b₃(demand−100) + b₄promotion + b₅lead×urban

The design row is [1,lead,urban,demand−100,promotion,lead×urban]. Multiply each element by its coefficient and sum. For a nonurban store the location and product terms vanish; for an urban store both contribute. The coefficients are in the earlier uncertainty table.

The fitted group lines compare the same demand and promotion scenario

The nonurban slope is 1.531 points/day and the urban slope is 1.759. These are estimated lines. Their apparent separation concerns level differences as well as slope differences; the slope test alone does not test whether the lines coincide.

Two complete four-day profiles differ by the main and interaction terms together

Difference = urban coefficient + 4 × interaction coefficient
Profile: demand 100, promotion .25Fitted rate
Nonurban, four days12.196%
Urban, four days14.106%
Urban minus nonurban1.910 points

Hold every other input fixed. The intercept, demand, and promotion terms cancel in the subtraction. This is a comparison of fitted baseline outcomes, which can inform which stores deserve a closer operating review.

Work through the reasoning gap

Worked application

Two residualizations reconstruct the adjusted delivery slope

Same 150 baseline stores and same six-column model
CalculationResult
Residual X against residual Y slope1.53
Delivery coefficient in full regression1.53

Compute rX=X−Zγ̂ and rY=Y−Zδ̂, then (rX′rY)/(rX′rX). The notebook reconstructs both residual vectors and verifies numerical equality with the full regression. Read this as the variation left after the other design columns have been accounted for. The observed overlap and available residual variation limit the precision of that comparison.

Covariance belongs in the uncertainty of a sum

Compute with unrounded entries; negative covariance can reduce the sum variance
Urban delivery-slope variance componentValue
Var(delivery coefficient)0.01
Var(interaction coefficient)0.03
Twice their covariance-0.03
Square root of their sum: SE0.10

The urban slope is b_delivery+b_interaction=1.759 points/day. Its variance is V11+V55+2V15 using the zero-based code indices. The HC1 normal-reference interval is 1.554 to 1.965. Adding standard errors, or adding the endpoints of two separate intervals, does not calculate this interval. The full covariance matrix expresses how the two estimates move together.

Explain the coefficient change with three regressions

Worked application

The omitted-variable identity names both ingredients of the change

Identical 150-store sample in all three fits
RegressionCoefficient
Rate on lead: short slope1.61872
Rate on lead and urban: lead slope1.68487
Rate on lead and urban: urban coefficient γ1.92295
Urban on lead: sorting slope δ-0.03440

The positive location coefficient says urban stores have higher fitted rates at a fixed delivery time in this additive model. The negative sorting slope says urban location becomes less common as delivery time rises. Their product pulls the short-model delivery slope downward.

The signs and arithmetic explain why the short slope is smaller

1.61872 ≈ 1.68487 + (1.92295 × -0.03440)

The product is -0.06615 points per day. Adding it to the longer-model slope recovers the short slope before rounding. This is the lead-plus-urban comparison, not the later model with demand, promotions, and an interaction. Naming each model prevents the arithmetic from being applied to unrelated coefficients.

Put uncertainty around the comparison that matters

Worked application

Centering delivery at three days gives the group coefficient a useful reference

Reference changes; fitted values and slope difference do not
Coefficient meaningLead uncenteredLead−3 centered
Urban difference at reference0.997 at zero days1.682 at three days
Lead×urban coefficient0.2280.228
PredictionsOriginal profilesIdentical profiles

Lead=0 is outside the observed two-to-five-day range. Replacing lead with lead−3 moves the urban coefficient to a supported operating value. The new intercept is the nonurban fitted value at three days, demand 100, and promotion zero. Centering changes coefficient meanings and their covariance, not the model’s predictions.

Meaningful group differences can be precise even when a reference coefficient is not

Contrasts hold demand and promotion fixed; units are percentage points
Lead daysUrban differenceHC1 SE95% interval
21.4540.3060.854 to 2.054
31.6820.1931.303 to 2.060
41.9100.1811.555 to 2.265
52.1390.2831.584 to 2.693

For lead L, the contrast row is [0,0,1,0,0,L]. Its estimate is cᵀb and its variance is cᵀVc. Coefficient covariance matters: adding separate interval endpoints does not construct the correct interval. The slope difference can be uncertain while differences at supported profiles are estimated precisely.

The joint test finds a group difference without establishing different slopes

Robust joint Wald χ²(2) = 118.33; p < 0.001

Test urban=0 and lead×urban=0 together, holding demand and promotion terms in the model. The computed p-value is 2.02e-26. The joint null of coincident lines is rejected, while the slope-only p-value is 0.156. The results answer different questions: the joint rejection can be driven by level differences.

Read uncertainty before comparing the richer model

Worked application

The lead coefficient is precise; the slope difference is less precise

Six-column model; normal-reference 95% intervals
TermEstimateHC1 SE95% interval
Intercept5.3370.4844.388 to 6.285
Lead1.5310.1211.293 to 1.769
Urban0.9970.602-0.182 to 2.176
Demand−1000.0590.0070.045 to 0.073
Promotion share2.9440.4871.989 to 3.899
Lead×urban0.2280.161-0.087 to 0.544

The lead coefficient is the slope for nonurban stores. The interaction estimates how much the urban slope differs. The urban main effect refers to lead=0 here; we will move that reference into the observed range. HC1 leaves the fitted coefficients unchanged.

The interaction estimate does not establish a slope difference at 5%

z = 0.228/0.161 = 1.418; two-sided p = 0.156

The null is that the two delivery slopes are equal after demand and promotion share are held fixed. Its 95% interval includes zero, so this test does not reject at 5%. The fitted slopes still differ numerically; neither a positive estimate nor a non-rejection settles whether the population slopes differ. Operational importance also depends on the size of a plausible difference.

A higher confidence level produces a wider interval from the same estimate

Same coefficient and HC1 SE; critical values 1.960 and 2.576
Term95% interval99% interval
Nonurban lead slope1.293 to 1.7691.218 to 1.843
Slope difference-0.087 to 0.544-0.186 to 0.643

The estimate does not change when the confidence level changes. A larger critical value gives wider coverage and a stricter matching two-sided test. The nonurban slope excludes zero at both levels; the slope difference includes zero at both.

Return to the simple line to see prediction uncertainty

Worked application

A new store’s rate has a wider interval than the average relationship

We deliberately use the two-column simple model here to expose the textbook calculation. It is the same line as Lesson 4, not the six-column model in the preceding table. Constant residual variance and a normal-error reference supply the classical individual interval. The uncertainty target is a new comparable eight-week store average.

The individual standard error adds residual variance before taking a square root

Student t critical value with 148 degrees of freedom
Four-day delivery profileCalculation
Fitted mean13.433%
Mean SE0.142 points
Residual variance2.611 points²
Individual SE√(2.611+0.142²) = 1.622
95% mean interval13.153 to 13.713%
95% individual interval10.228 to 16.638%

Multiply each standard error by the same t critical value, then add and subtract from the same fitted mean. Residual variance is in squared rate points, so it is added to squared mean SE before taking the square root. This calculation connects the two bands to quantities that students can reconstruct.

Add complexity for a defined comparison

Worked application

Adjusted R-squared accounts for parameters consumed by the fit

Adjusted R² = 1 − [SSE/(n−p)] / [SST/(n−1)]

Here p counts every estimated coefficient, including the intercept. Ordinary training R² cannot decrease when independent columns are added to a nested OLS model on the same rows. Adjusted R² can decrease because it accounts for the degrees of freedom used. Neither statistic estimates future forecasting accuracy.

The same-sample comparison separates fit gains from extra parameters

150 rows throughout; RMSE in rate points
ModelpR²Adjusted R²RMSE
Lead only20.5480.5451.605
Add urban30.7090.7051.287
Add demand / promo50.8210.8161.010
Group slopes60.8240.8181.002
Add demand squared70.8280.8200.991

The additive model includes lead, urban, demand, and promotions. The group-slopes model then adds lead×urban. The final model adds centered demand squared. The table evaluates training fit; Lesson 6 evaluates forecasting procedures on later data.

A quadratic extends the controlled model with a changing demand slope

Added term: -0.0857 × [(demand−100)/10]²

Keep all six earlier columns and add the square. In this model the demand slope is 0.0714 + 2×(-0.0857)×(demand−100)/100 points per index unit. Interpret the linear and squared terms together. The fit comparison shows the actual gain in these stores, rather than assuming a more flexible specification must be operationally better.

Use model errors to choose the next practical inquiry

Worked application

Above the diagonal means more stockouts than the model fits

A residual is observed minus fitted. Read its sign from the stated axes. The original hotel plot put observed values on the horizontal axis, so its above/below interpretation was reversed; this lesson consistently uses fitted horizontal and observed vertical.

Residuals identify stores whose observed outcomes need another explanation

Largest positive residuals from the six-column model
StoreObservedFittedResidual
S02318.3015.183.12
S13716.6114.631.98
S06211.529.601.92
S05512.8610.961.90
S12017.3215.511.81

For these stores, inspect delivery disruptions, unrecorded practices, and measurement. The residual shortlist asks where to learn more; it does not establish who caused the difference. Keep the outcome period and compared profile visible during that conversation.

A residual plot asks whether unexplained spread changes with the fitted rate

Look for systematic curvature, changing spread, or individual records that deserve investigation. Robust SEs address coefficient uncertainty under unequal variance, but they do not remove a missing mean pattern. Review the model and records together before expanding the operating use.

Decide where this comparison can be used next

Worked application

Use the baseline comparison to design a testable operating review

  • Report a complete profile and its uncertainty
  • Distinguish group-level differences from slope differences
  • Investigate stores with large residuals
  • Check transfer before using the model in a new setting

Suppose a new region has seven-day delivery cycles and a different promotion system. Those profiles extend beyond the observed delivery range and change the operating setting. Start by collecting comparable outcomes and validating the relationship there. For existing stores, Lesson 6 will turn the explanatory inputs into a procedure that can be evaluated before next week’s outcomes are known.

Explain, reconstruct, diagnose and transfer

Decision and synthesis

Reconstruct the calculation before inspecting the worked answer

  • Remove the other columns from both delivery and stockouts, fit the residual slope, and compare with the full model.
  • For an urban slope b1+b5, an analyst adds the two standard errors. Replace this with a covariance calculation.

Work independently or explain your reasoning to a partner. State the target, units and assumptions before calculating. The student notebook provides runnable setup and separate task cells; the companion solution checks the calculation. The lesson’s completed lab remains available as a reference, with its steps separated into smaller cells.

Transfer the method and defend the decision

  • The same stores are observed for 12 weeks. Which uncertainty method would allow within-store dependence, and what must still hold between stores?
  • Submit a calculation, an assumption and a justified next action

An acceptable answer can recommend more information, a narrower claim or no action. It must connect the method to the target and explain the consequence of a failed assumption. Use the assessment criteria after attempting the task; matching a supplied recommendation is not the grading objective.

After your attempt: check the reasoning

Open the assessment criteria

Reproduce the full coefficient with both residualizations; include 2V15. Name the reference group in the interaction model. Clustering requires enough independent store clusters.

Update the decision memo

Report adjusted profile differences with their uncertainty. The fitted delivery slopes are 1.531 and 1.759 points/day, but their difference is not established at 5%. The joint test and supported profile contrasts show location-related differences. Use the residual shortlist to guide operating review and validate any forecasting use.

Make the call

How can the group-lines joint test reject while the slope-difference test does not?

Compare your reasoning

The joint test asks whether both level and slope differences are zero. A level difference can drive its rejection even when the slope difference is imprecise. State which comparison each test addresses.

The bigger picture

Multiple regression makes comparisons more specific. Its interpretation depends on the included variables, coding, reference values, and interactions. Use fully specified profiles to explain the model in any application, and distinguish uncertainty about a coefficient, a mean response, and a new individual outcome.

After your decision: open the known answer

The baseline mechanism includes a delivery-by-location interaction. Its known presence does not guarantee that a particular sample yields a statistically significant estimate. Compare the estimate and interval with the mechanism only after interpreting the observed data.
